title: Farxiga and Alcohol: Ketoacidosis Risk, Dehydration and Safe Limits
excerpt: Can you drink alcohol on Farxiga (dapagliflozin)? How heavy drinking raises ketoacidosis and dehydration risk, why your prescriber sets the limit, and the warning signs that need care.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Farxiga? How alcohol raises ketoacidosis and dehydration risk with dapagliflozin, who sets your limit, and warning signs that need a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Farxiga (dapagliflozin) doesn't react chemically with alcohol, and its label doesn't tell you to avoid drinking altogether. The concern is what heavy drinking does on top of the way Farxiga works. The medicine makes you lose sugar and water through your urine, and it nudges your body toward burning fat. Heavy alcohol use pushes in the same directions. Together they raise the risk of **ketoacidosis**, a rare but serious build-up of acid in the blood that, on this type of drug, can happen even when your blood sugar reading looks normal. They also add up to more dehydration and dizziness. For most people whose doctor is comfortable with it, an occasional drink with food is a very different situation from a binge on an empty stomach.

**The quick rules:** Ask the doctor who prescribed Farxiga whether alcohol is OK for you. If it is, stay within the limit they set, drink with a meal, have water between drinks, and skip binges. Don't drink heavily while fasting, on a strict keto or very low-carb diet, or while you're sick. If you're vomiting or can't keep food and fluids down after a night out, contact your care team, because that's when Farxiga gets risky. If you have stomach pain, keep vomiting, feel unusually weak, or are breathing fast and deep, get emergency care and tell them you take Farxiga.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and the official US prescribing information for dapagliflozin. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, and you should not stop or change your Farxiga dose on your own. **Talk to your doctor before drinking alcohol on Farxiga**, especially if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, take it for heart failure or kidney disease, use a diuretic (water pill), follow a low-carb diet, or tend to have more than a couple of drinks at a time. **Get emergency care (call 911 in the US) if** you have nausea or vomiting that won't stop, stomach pain, unusual tiredness or weakness, fast or labored breathing, or confusion, even if your blood sugar is normal.

## What Farxiga Is and Who Takes It

Farxiga is the brand name for **dapagliflozin**, a once-a-day tablet. It belongs to a family of medicines called **SGLT2 inhibitors**, also called "gliflozins." Jardiance (empagliflozin) and Invokana (canagliflozin) are in the same family.

Farxiga is unusual because a lot of the people who take it don't have diabetes. In the US it is approved to:

- Lower blood sugar in people with **type 2 diabetes**, alongside diet and exercise
- Lower the risk of hospital stays for heart failure in adults with type 2 diabetes and heart disease or heart risk factors
- Lower the risk of death and hospital stays in adults with **heart failure**
- Slow the decline of kidney function and lower related risks in adults with **chronic kidney disease** who are at risk of it getting worse

Those heart and kidney approvals came out of large clinical trials (known as DECLARE-TIMI 58, DAPA-HF, DAPA-CKD, and DELIVER). The practical point for this article is that "Farxiga and alcohol" isn't only a diabetes question. If you take Farxiga for your heart or kidneys, the same alcohol cautions apply, and a couple of them, like fluid balance, matter even more.

## How Farxiga Works, in Plain Words

Your kidneys filter your blood all day. Sugar gets filtered out along with water and salt, and then the kidneys reabsorb almost all of that sugar so you don't waste it. A transport protein called **SGLT2**, found in the first part of the kidney's tubes, does most of the reabsorbing. It also pulls sodium back in at the same time.

Farxiga blocks SGLT2. So:

- **More sugar leaves in your urine.** That lowers blood sugar without making your pancreas pump out more insulin.
- **More water and salt leave too.** Sugar in the urine drags water with it, so you pee more, especially in the first weeks. This mild water-pill effect is part of why the drug helps in heart failure.
- **Your body leans more on fat for fuel.** Losing sugar through the kidneys shifts your metabolism a little toward burning fat, which produces **ketones**. Normally they stay at a low, harmless level.
- **Hormones shift slightly.** Insulin tends to drift down and glucagon (the hormone that raises blood sugar) up. That shift is part of why ketones rise on this drug.

Alcohol affects your fluid balance, your blood sugar, and your ketone levels too. That overlap is the whole story of Farxiga and alcohol. It isn't that one drug blocks the breakdown of the other. It's that both push the same levers.

## The Main Risk: Ketoacidosis

If you remember one section, make it this one.

### What ketoacidosis is

Ketones are acids. When the body can't use sugar properly, usually because there isn't enough insulin around, it starts burning fat very quickly and ketones pile up faster than they can be cleared. The blood becomes too acidic. That condition is called **ketoacidosis**, and it is a medical emergency that usually needs hospital treatment with fluids, insulin, and close monitoring.

### Why it's harder to spot on Farxiga

The FDA added warnings about ketoacidosis to every SGLT2 inhibitor label in 2015, and the Farxiga label carries it today. It's uncommon, but it has a dangerous twist. On SGLT2 inhibitors, ketoacidosis can happen while blood sugar is **normal or only a little high**. Doctors call this **euglycemic ketoacidosis** ("euglycemic" just means normal blood sugar).

Most people who manage diabetes learn that very high sugar readings are the warning sign. On Farxiga, the drug keeps sending sugar out through your urine, so your meter can read 140 or 180 while ketones climb. People without diabetes who take Farxiga for heart failure or kidney disease may not own a meter at all, and may never have heard the word ketoacidosis. The warning still appears on the label for everyone who takes it.

### Where alcohol fits in

The Farxiga prescribing information lists factors that make ketoacidosis more likely. They include a sudden cut in calories or fasting, acute illness, surgery, a drop in insulin dose, problems with the pancreas making insulin, and **alcohol abuse**. The patient medication guide says it in everyday terms: drinking a lot of alcohol.

Heavy drinking adds to the risk in three ways:

1. **Breaking down alcohol changes the liver's chemistry.** While the liver is processing a large amount of alcohol, it is slower to make new glucose and more inclined to make ketones. Heavy drinking can cause a ketone-related emergency all on its own, called alcoholic ketoacidosis, even in people who take no medicine at all.
2. **Drinking often replaces eating.** Skipping dinner, drinking on an empty stomach, or not being able to face food the next morning all cut your carbohydrate intake. Eating very little is its own risk factor on the label.
3. **Vomiting and dehydration pile on.** A night that ends in vomiting means lost fluid, no food staying down, and stress hormones that raise ketones further. A dried-out body also clears ketones less well.

A binge, no dinner, and a morning of vomiting is close to the textbook setup for ketoacidosis on an SGLT2 inhibitor. One beer with a burger is not.

### Warning signs

The Farxiga label tells patients to stop taking it and get medical help right away if they have symptoms of ketoacidosis, which include:

- Nausea or vomiting
- Pain in the stomach area
- Unusual tiredness or weakness
- Trouble breathing or fast, deep breathing
- Feeling confused or very sleepy

Some people also notice a fruity smell on the breath, a classic sign of high ketones.

Look at that list next to a hangover. Nausea, a sore stomach, and wiped-out tiredness are what a bad morning after feels like. That's exactly why this is easy to miss. A normal hangover slowly gets better through the day as you drink water and eat. If yours is getting worse, you can't keep anything down, or your breathing feels heavy or fast, don't sleep it off. Get checked, and tell the staff you take Farxiga so they test your ketones and blood acid levels and not just your sugar.

## Farxiga, Alcohol, and Dehydration

Both Farxiga and alcohol make you lose fluid, by different routes.

- **Farxiga** sends extra water out with the sugar in your urine. The label warns about **volume depletion**, meaning low body fluid. That can show up as dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting, especially when you stand up quickly. It's more likely in older adults, in people with reduced kidney function or low blood pressure, and in people who also take a loop diuretic such as furosemide (Lasix).
- **Alcohol** blocks vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of that signal, you urinate more than you drink. That's why you wake up parched after a night out. Our explainer on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers the details.

Put them together and the losses stack. You might notice:

- More trips to the bathroom during the night
- Dizziness or a head rush when you stand up
- A heavier headache and drier mouth the next day
- Blood pressure lower than your usual, especially if you also take blood pressure medicine

The fix is mostly about doing the obvious things on purpose: water between drinks, a glass before bed, and steady fluids the next morning. If you're vomiting and can't keep fluids down, that's a reason to call your care team rather than wait.

### If you take Farxiga for heart failure

Fluid is a balancing act in heart failure. Too little and you get dizzy and your kidneys suffer; too much and fluid backs up into your lungs and legs. If your heart team has given you a daily fluid limit, follow their numbers rather than general "drink lots of water" hangover advice, and ask them how to handle drinking days. Alcohol is also hard on the heart muscle itself when used heavily over time, which works against the reason you take Farxiga. Many heart failure teams advise limiting alcohol or avoiding it, so this is one to raise directly at your next appointment.

### If you take Farxiga for kidney disease

When your kidneys are already working at reduced capacity, dehydration hits them harder. A short-term dip in kidney function from being dried out is a known concern on SGLT2 inhibitors, and the label advises checking kidney function and watching for low fluid. Heavy drinking that ends in vomiting is exactly the kind of fluid loss that can tip things over. Our guide to [alcohol and kidney function](/never-hungover/alcohol-kidney-disease-renal-function-impact-2025) explains how drinking affects the kidneys more broadly.

## Farxiga, Alcohol, and Low Blood Sugar

On its own, Farxiga rarely causes low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), because it lowers sugar through your urine and doesn't force your pancreas to release insulin. People who take it for heart or kidney disease without diabetes are very unlikely to have lows from Farxiga.

The picture changes if you take Farxiga alongside other diabetes medicines. The label notes that the risk of low blood sugar rises when it's combined with **insulin** or with **insulin secretagogues**, the drugs that push the pancreas to release insulin. The common ones are sulfonylureas such as glipizide, glyburide, and glimepiride. Lower doses of those medicines may be needed.

Alcohol adds to that risk. While your liver is busy clearing alcohol, it's slower to release stored sugar and make new sugar. That can last for hours, which is why drinking-related lows often happen overnight or the next morning.

If you're in that group:

- Eat food with some carbohydrates while you drink.
- Check your blood sugar before bed, and have a snack if it's on the low side.
- Make sure someone you're with knows you have diabetes. A low can look a lot like being drunk, and the people around you may not realize you need sugar.
- Ask your doctor whether to adjust anything on days you plan to drink.

Our guide to [managing blood sugar when you drink](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) explains how beer, wine, and spirits affect glucose differently.

## Can You Drink on Farxiga? Your Prescriber Sets the Limit

The Farxiga label doesn't ban alcohol. It warns about heavy use. Whether any amount is fine for you depends on why you take Farxiga, your kidney function, your other medicines, and how stable your condition is. That's why the prescribing doctor is the right person to decide.

General diabetes guidance doesn't ban alcohol, but it isn't a personal limit on Farxiga, which adds its own ketoacidosis and dehydration risks. The amount that's okay for you, if any, should come from the doctor who prescribes it, and it may be lower or zero if you have heart failure or kidney disease. When you talk about it, count in standard drinks: in the US that's about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits.

If your doctor is fine with an occasional drink, these habits keep the risk lower:

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Drink with a meal that includes some carbohydrates | Drinking on an empty stomach or instead of a meal |
| Have a glass of water between drinks | Binge drinking or drinking fast to catch up |
| Pick lower-sugar options like dry wine, light beer, or spirits with a zero-sugar mixer | Sweet cocktails, big pours, and sugary mixers |
| Check your blood sugar if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea | Drinking when you're already sick, vomiting, or not eating |
| Tell someone you're with that you take Farxiga | Heavy drinking while fasting or on strict keto |

### Low-carb diets, fasting, and alcohol

Cutting carbs is common and often helpful in type 2 diabetes. But very low-carb and ketogenic diets raise ketone levels by design, and fasting does the same. Each of those is a ketoacidosis risk factor with Farxiga. Add a night of heavy drinking and you're stacking three pushes in the same direction. If you follow a strict low-carb plan or do intermittent fasting, mention it to your doctor specifically, and be most careful with alcohol on those days. Our article on [how alcohol affects ketosis](/never-hungover/alcohol-ketogenic-diet-ketosis-impact-analysis-2025) goes into the overlap.

## How Long After Taking Farxiga Can You Drink?

This is one of the most common questions, and the honest answer is that spacing things out doesn't help much.

Farxiga is taken once a day, and the label puts its half-life (the time for the amount in your blood to fall by half) at roughly 13 hours. Because you take it every day, there's always some in your system, and its effect on your kidneys carries through the whole day. Taking your pill in the morning and drinking in the evening doesn't create a safe gap, and skipping a dose to "make room" for a night out isn't recommended unless your doctor tells you to.

What matters more than the clock:

- **How much** you drink
- **Whether you've eaten** that day
- **Whether you're well** or already sick, dehydrated, or not eating

A drink with dinner is a lower-risk situation whatever time you took your tablet. A binge on an empty stomach is risky no matter when you took it.

## Sick Days, Surgery, and Pausing Farxiga

These rules are worth knowing whether or not you drink.

**Sick days.** Many care teams give people on SGLT2 inhibitors "sick-day rules." The usual idea is to pause the medicine temporarily if you're unwell enough that you can't eat or drink normally, for example with vomiting, diarrhea, fever, or dehydration, and restart once you're eating and drinking again. A day of vomiting after a heavy night counts as a sick day. The details vary, especially for people who use insulin or take Farxiga for heart failure, so ask for your own written plan.

**Surgery and procedures.** The Farxiga label advises stopping it at least 3 days before scheduled surgery, because fasting and the stress of surgery raise ketoacidosis risk. Your surgical team should tell you when to stop and when to restart. Mention any drinking to them as well.

**Don't quit on your own.** For many people Farxiga lowers the risk of heart failure hospital stays and slows kidney decline. If you find alcohol and this medicine don't fit together in your life, talk it through with your doctor rather than quietly stopping the tablet.

## Farxiga, Alcohol, and Urinary or Genital Infections

This part rarely comes up in alcohol articles, but it's relevant. Because Farxiga puts sugar in your urine, it raises the risk of **genital yeast infections** and **urinary tract infections**, both listed on the label. Rarely, it's been linked to a serious infection of the skin and tissue around the genitals called **Fournier's gangrene**, which needs urgent care.

Alcohol doesn't cause these infections. But heavy drinking can lead to dehydration (concentrated urine), less attention to hygiene, and delays in noticing symptoms. If you're treated for a UTI while on Farxiga, the antibiotic may carry its own alcohol cautions. Our guide to [drinking on UTI antibiotics](/never-hungover/uti-antibiotics-and-alcohol) explains which ones matter.

**See a doctor promptly if you have** burning when you pee, fever, or pain in your side or back, or any pain, tenderness, redness, or swelling in the genital area or the skin between the genitals and the back passage, especially with fever or feeling generally unwell.

## Xigduo XR and Qtern: Combination Pills and Alcohol

Dapagliflozin also comes combined with other diabetes medicines in a single tablet. If you take one of these, the alcohol cautions for both ingredients apply.

- **Xigduo XR (dapagliflozin plus metformin).** Metformin carries a boxed warning about **lactic acidosis**, another rare build-up of acid in the blood, and its labeling warns that alcohol increases metformin's effect on lactate. Patients are told to avoid excessive alcohol. That means two separate acid-related risks, ketoacidosis from dapagliflozin and lactic acidosis from metformin, both get worse with heavy drinking. Our [metformin and alcohol](/never-hungover/metformin-and-alcohol) guide covers the metformin side.
- **Qtern (dapagliflozin plus saxagliptin).** Saxagliptin is a DPP-4 inhibitor that on its own rarely causes low blood sugar. The main alcohol concerns are the dapagliflozin ones: ketoacidosis and dehydration.

## Is Farxiga Different From Jardiance or Other SGLT2 Inhibitors?

Not in any way that changes the alcohol advice. The ketoacidosis warning covers the whole class, so the same cautions apply to:

- **Jardiance** (empagliflozin), which we cover in our [Jardiance and alcohol](/never-hungover/jardiance-and-alcohol) guide
- **Invokana** (canagliflozin)
- **Steglatro** (ertugliflozin)
- **Inpefa** (sotagliflozin)

The labels differ in details such as approved uses, dosing, and kidney function cut-offs, but the message on alcohol is the same: heavy drinking raises ketoacidosis risk, and dehydration is a shared concern. If you've switched from one to another, your drinking advice doesn't need to change.

## Does Alcohol Make Farxiga Less Effective?

Alcohol doesn't stop dapagliflozin from blocking SGLT2 in your kidneys. But drinking can work against the reasons you take it:

- **Sugary drinks can outrun the drug.** Sweet cocktails, dessert wines, ciders, and regular soda mixers can push your blood sugar up more than Farxiga offsets.
- **Alcohol adds empty calories**, which can cancel out the modest weight loss many people see on SGLT2 inhibitors.
- **Regular heavy drinking raises blood pressure** and, over time, can weaken the heart muscle. That runs directly against heart failure treatment.
- **Heavy drinking is linked to fatty liver** and worse long-term diabetes control.

So the effect isn't on the pill. It's on your blood sugar, weight, heart, and kidneys, which are the things Farxiga is meant to protect. If you also take a blood pressure medicine like an ACE inhibitor, our [lisinopril and alcohol](/never-hungover/lisinopril-and-alcohol) guide explains how that combination adds to dizziness.

## The Farxiga Hangover: Why the Morning After Can Feel Worse

People on Farxiga sometimes say their hangovers feel worse than before. That fits the biology. You start the night a little drier than someone not on the drug, alcohol drains more fluid, and by morning you may be short on both fluid and carbohydrates.

To make the next day easier and safer:

- **Rehydrate early.** Water first. An electrolyte drink helps if you've been sweating or vomiting; pick a low-sugar one if you watch your glucose, and check with your heart team if you have a fluid or salt limit.
- **Eat breakfast.** Even if you feel rough. Food steadies blood sugar and helps keep ketones from building up.
- **Check your numbers if you have the tools.** Test blood sugar if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea. If your care team gave you a ketone meter or urine strips and you feel unwell, use them. A blood ketone meter gives a more current reading than urine strips. Ask your doctor ahead of time what level should prompt a call.
- **Don't trust a normal glucose reading on its own.** On Farxiga, ketoacidosis can happen with normal sugar.
- **Watch the direction.** A normal hangover gets better as the day goes on. One that gets worse, keeps you vomiting, or changes your breathing needs medical attention.

## When to See a Doctor

**Call your doctor or care team soon if:**

- You've been vomiting, or can't eat or drink normally, for more than a few hours
- You regularly have more than a couple of drinks at a time while on Farxiga
- You feel dizzy or faint when you stand, or your blood pressure is lower than usual
- You've had low blood sugar episodes after drinking
- You have symptoms of a urinary or genital infection

**Get emergency care right away (call 911 in the US) if you have:**

- Nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain that's severe or getting worse
- Fast, deep, or labored breathing
- Confusion, extreme sleepiness, or trouble staying awake
- Weakness or tiredness far beyond a normal hangover
- A low blood sugar you can't bring up, or someone with diabetes who won't respond
- Fainting, or signs of severe dehydration such as very little urine and a racing heart
- Pain, swelling, or redness in the genital area with fever

Tell the medical team you take Farxiga (dapagliflozin) so they check ketones and blood acid levels, even if your sugar is normal.

## Can a Supplement Help?

Some people who drink now and then look at supplements to soften the morning after. Here's an honest take, and it matters far less than the basics above.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited data in people. There is no good evidence that DHM lowers the risk of ketoacidosis, dehydration, or low blood sugar on Farxiga, and it does not make heavy drinking safe on this medicine. It also hasn't been studied in people taking SGLT2 inhibitors, so check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding it, as you would with any supplement, particularly if you have kidney disease. If you and your doctor decide it's reasonable for an occasional night out, a well-reviewed option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and the premium [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) adds other ingredients. Read the full label for added sugars or anything your care team would want to know about. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers how DHM fits with common prescriptions, and the [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing.

The bigger wins are free: drink less, eat with your drinks, alternate with water, and know the warning signs. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, and our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications) covers other common prescriptions.

## The Bottom Line

- Farxiga doesn't react with alcohol directly, and the label doesn't ban drinking. It warns against **heavy** alcohol use.
- The main risk is **ketoacidosis**, which on Farxiga can happen with normal blood sugar. Heavy drinking, not eating, vomiting, fasting, low-carb diets, and illness all raise it.
- Farxiga and alcohol both drain fluid, so **dehydration and dizziness** are more likely, which matters most in heart failure and kidney disease.
- **Low blood sugar** is mainly a concern if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea.
- Timing your pill around drinks doesn't help much. Amount, food, and whether you're well matter more.
- Ask your doctor what's safe for you, learn your sick-day rules, and don't stop Farxiga on your own.

Farxiga is often prescribed alongside, or instead of, the GLP-1 medicines. If you take one of those, our guides to [Wegovy and alcohol](/never-hungover/wegovy-and-alcohol), [Mounjaro and alcohol](/never-hungover/mounjaro-and-alcohol), [Zepbound and alcohol](/never-hungover/zepbound-and-alcohol), and the [Ozempic and GLP-1 research guide](/never-hungover/ozempic-glp1-alcohol-hangover-2026-research-guide) cover how they interact with drinking.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Farxiga?**

Many people on Farxiga can have an occasional drink if their doctor agrees. There's no direct chemical interaction, and the label doesn't ban alcohol, but it warns that heavy drinking raises the risk of ketoacidosis, a serious build-up of acid in the blood. If your doctor says it's OK, drink with a meal, have water between drinks, and avoid binges. Ask first if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea, or take Farxiga for heart failure or kidney disease.

**Does alcohol increase the risk of ketoacidosis on Farxiga?**

Heavy drinking does. The Farxiga prescribing information lists alcohol abuse as a factor that makes ketoacidosis more likely, along with fasting or eating very little, acute illness, and surgery. Alcohol shifts the liver toward making ketones, and heavy nights often come with skipped meals and vomiting, which add to the risk. On SGLT2 inhibitors, ketoacidosis can happen with normal blood sugar, so don't rely on a glucose reading alone.

**What are the signs of ketoacidosis on Farxiga?**

Nausea or vomiting, stomach pain, unusual tiredness or weakness, fast or deep breathing, trouble breathing, and confusion or extreme sleepiness. Some people notice a fruity smell on the breath. These overlap with a bad hangover, which is why they're easy to miss. If symptoms are severe, getting worse, or include breathing changes, get emergency care and tell the team you take Farxiga so they check ketones and blood acid levels.

**How long after taking Farxiga can I drink alcohol?**

Timing doesn't make much difference. Farxiga is taken once a day and has a half-life of roughly 13 hours, so there's always some in your system. How much you drink, whether you've eaten, and whether you're well matter far more than when you took your tablet. Don't skip doses to make room for drinking unless your doctor tells you to.

**Can Farxiga and alcohol cause dehydration?**

Yes. Farxiga sends sugar into your urine, which pulls water with it, and alcohol blocks the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. Together they can leave you dehydrated, dizzy, or lightheaded, especially when standing up. Drink water between drinks and the next morning. If you have heart failure and a fluid limit, follow your heart team's numbers.

**Can I drink alcohol if I take Farxiga for heart failure or kidney disease?**

Ask your doctor first, because the answer depends on how stable your condition is. The ketoacidosis warning applies whether or not you have diabetes, and dehydration is harder on weakened kidneys and on fluid balance in heart failure. Heavy drinking over time also strains the heart muscle, which works against your treatment. Many heart and kidney teams advise keeping alcohol low or avoiding it.

**Is it safe to drink alcohol on Xigduo XR?**

Xigduo XR combines dapagliflozin with metformin, so both sets of warnings apply. Heavy drinking raises the risk of ketoacidosis from the dapagliflozin and lactic acidosis from the metformin, and patients are told to avoid excessive alcohol. Whether any alcohol is okay for you, and how much, is for your doctor to decide.

**Does alcohol cause low blood sugar with Farxiga?**

Farxiga alone rarely causes low blood sugar. The risk rises if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide or glimepiride, and alcohol adds to it by slowing the liver's release of sugar for hours, including overnight. If you take those medicines, eat while you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and ask your doctor whether to adjust anything on drinking days.

**Should I stop taking Farxiga if I plan to drink?**

Don't stop Farxiga on your own. For many people it protects the heart and kidneys as well as lowering blood sugar. Ask your doctor whether any alcohol is OK for you, what limit to stay under, and what your sick-day rules are. Many care teams advise pausing SGLT2 inhibitors temporarily if you're vomiting or can't eat or drink normally, then restarting once you're well.

faq.answer: Xigduo XR combines dapagliflozin with metformin, so both sets of warnings apply. Heavy drinking raises the risk of ketoacidosis from the dapagliflozin and lactic acidosis from the metformin, and patients are told to avoid excessive alcohol. Whether any alcohol is okay for you, and how much, is for your doctor to decide.

faq.question: Does alcohol cause low blood sugar with Farxiga?
faq.answer: Farxiga alone rarely causes low blood sugar. The risk rises if you also take insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide or glimepiride, and alcohol adds to it by slowing the liver's release of sugar for hours, including overnight. If you take those medicines, eat while you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and ask your doctor whether to adjust anything on drinking days.

faq.question: Should I stop taking Farxiga if I plan to drink?
faq.answer: Don't stop Farxiga on your own. For many people it protects the heart and kidneys as well as lowering blood sugar. Ask your doctor whether any alcohol is OK for you, what limit to stay under, and what your sick-day rules are. Many care teams advise pausing SGLT2 inhibitors temporarily if you're vomiting or can't eat or drink normally, then restarting once you're well.
